title: Consumer Vibe Check: Gas Prices and Inflation Expectations - San Francisco Fed
gist: Using New York Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations panel data from June 2013 to June 2025, SF Fed researchers find household inflation expectations ratchet asymmetrically with gasoline: a 10 percentage point upward revision in expected gas price growth coincides with a 0.24 percentage point rise in one-year inflation expectations, while comparable downward revisions produce no statistically significant decline. The effect is more than three times larger for households earning under $50,000 than for those over $100,000, and upward gas revisions also widen perceived inflation uncertainty by 3.3%.

insights.claim: Average U.S. monthly retail gasoline prices hit $4.65 per gallon in May 2026, up from $3.06 in February 2026 before the start of the U.S.-Iran conflict — a roughly 52% move in three months.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: A pump-price move of this size is the exact stimulus this research shows ratchets household inflation expectations upward without symmetric reversal — watch breakevens and survey expectations even if oil retraces.

insights.claim: A 10 percentage point upward revision in a household's expected gasoline price growth is associated with a 0.24 percentage point increase in that same household's one-year inflation expectations — statistically significant but quantitatively modest.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
entities: New York Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations
insights.so_what: Gives a usable elasticity: a doubling of pump-price expectations moves one-year household inflation expectations by only a few tenths, so gas shocks alone are unlikely to de-anchor expectations absent other pressure.
insights.quote: A 10 percentage point upward revision in expected gas price growth is associated with a 0.24 percentage point increase in one-year inflation expectations.

insights.claim: Downward revisions in expected gasoline price growth are not associated with a statistically significant decline in inflation expectations, and the gap between the upward and downward responses is statistically distinguishable from zero.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: Energy disinflation does not buy back the expectations damage that energy inflation caused — a falling oil price is a weaker policy tailwind for the Fed than a rising one is a headwind.
insights.quote: A comparable downward revision is not associated with a statistically significant decline in inflation expectations

insights.claim: The core mental model is a one-way ratchet: gasoline price pressure leaves a more persistent imprint on household inflation outlooks when prices climb than when they subside.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
insights.so_what: Model energy pass-through to expectations as path-dependent, not mean-reverting — a round trip in oil leaves the expectations level higher than where it started.
insights.quote: Our results suggest that gasoline price pressures may leave a more persistent imprint on household inflation outlooks when prices climb than when they subside.

insights.claim: Households appear to treat sharp gasoline price increases as a signal about economy-wide inflation rather than as a change in one spending category, because gas is among the most salient and volatile expenses consumers face.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: Salience, not budget weight alone, drives the signal — so highly visible posted prices (fuel, groceries) carry outsized weight in expectations relative to their CPI share.
insights.quote: When gas prices rise sharply, people may interpret the increase not just as a price change in this category but as a signal about inflation more generally.
insights.locator: Gasoline prices are among the most salient

insights.claim: The observed comovement between gasoline and inflation expectations is repeatedly characterized as modest in magnitude, tempering the popular narrative that pump prices dominate consumer inflation psychology.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: Counterweight to trading gas prices as a proxy for expectations de-anchoring — the direction is real but the size argues against overreacting to a single pump-price spike.
insights.quote: quantitatively, the evidence suggests a moderate relationship between changes in expected gasoline prices and households’ inflation expectations

insights.claim: A 10 percentage point upward revision in expected gasoline price growth is associated with a 3.3% increase in the interquartile range of a household's one-year inflation expectations, versus only 1.4% for a comparable downward revision.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: Uncertainty is a separate, larger channel than the level effect — rising gas prices widen the distribution of expected outcomes, which supports higher inflation risk premia even when point forecasts barely move.
insights.quote: a 10 percentage point upward revision in expected gas-price growth is associated with a 3.3% increase in the IQR of one-year inflation expectations, while a comparable downward revision is associated with a 1.4% increase

insights.claim: Revisions to expected gasoline price growth in either direction — up or down — raise perceived inflation uncertainty, meaning falling gas price expectations still widen the distribution of outcomes households consider plausible.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: Energy volatility per se, not just direction, is the uncertainty driver — an oil price collapse does not restore confidence in the inflation outlook, arguing for persistently elevated inflation optionality pricing.

insights.claim: Concerns about gasoline prices can coincide with a materially less certain household inflation outlook even when the average change in expected inflation itself is small.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: Point-estimate survey measures understate the true expectations damage from energy shocks — track dispersion and IQR measures, not just median expected inflation.

insights.claim: The gasoline-to-inflation expectations pass-through is more than three times larger for households earning under $50,000 a year (0.38 percentage point per 10 point revision) than for those earning over $100,000 (0.12 percentage point), with the middle income group at 0.24 percentage point.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: Energy shocks hit expectations hardest exactly where balance sheets are thinnest — a leading indicator for discretionary spending pullback and low-income consumer credit stress when pump prices climb.
insights.quote: The relationship is therefore more than three times larger for households in the lowest income group than for those in the highest income group.

insights.claim: The education gradient runs the same direction but is flatter: 0.32 percentage point for high school graduates, 0.26 for some college, and 0.21 for college graduates per 10 percentage point upward revision in expected gasoline price growth.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: Income, not schooling, is the sharper sorting variable for expectations sensitivity, pointing at budget-share exposure rather than financial literacy as the operative mechanism.

insights.claim: The proposed mechanism for the income gradient is budget share: gasoline takes up a larger fraction of lower-income households' total spending, is harder to absorb without cutting other expenses, and therefore acts as a stronger signal about their overall cost of living.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: Implies substitution pressure: when gas expectations rise, the low-income cohort is the one that reallocates spending away from discretionary categories first.
insights.quote: higher gas prices may be harder for these households to absorb without cutting back on other expenses

insights.claim: The asymmetry holds universally across the income distribution — downward revisions to expected gasoline price growth produce no statistically meaningful decline in inflation expectations for any income group, not just for vulnerable households.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: The ratchet is a general feature of household belief formation, so falling energy prices cannot be counted on to pull aggregate expectations back down at any income tier.
insights.quote: downward revisions to expected gas price growth are not associated with statistically meaningful declines in inflation expectations for any income group
insights.locator: Although the comovement remains modest in absolute terms

insights.claim: The findings rest on the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations, monthly from June 2013 through June 2025, restricted to respondents with at least eight consecutive months of participation — a filter that retains about 70% of respondent-month observations.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
entities: New York Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations
Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
insights.so_what: A 12-year panel with high retention means the asymmetry is a structural regularity across multiple energy cycles, not an artifact of the 2022 or 2026 episodes.
insights.locator: The data cover monthly surveys from June 2013

insights.claim: The regression compares each respondent with themselves over time via individual baselines, so persistent cross-person differences — such as people who chronically report higher inflation — cannot drive the estimated comovement.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: The within-person design is why this evidence is stronger than aggregate survey correlations, which conflate common news shocks and shifting respondent composition.
insights.quote: we measure the relationship by comparing each person with themselves over time, rather than comparing people with one another
insights.locator: We then use a statistical method known as regression

insights.claim: Movements in aggregate survey averages are explicitly rejected as evidence that any individual's gas and inflation beliefs move together, since averages can comove because of common economic news or changes in the mix of survey respondents.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: A methodological warning for anyone reading headline University of Michigan or SCE aggregates as proof of energy pass-through — composition effects can manufacture the correlation.
insights.locator: This analysis requires a survey that follows the same respondents

insights.claim: The observational panel results align with prior experimental evidence from Aidala et al. (2024) on gasoline price changes and consumer inflation expectations, and extend an earlier SF Fed line of work by Glick et al. (2021) on commodity surges and household inflation expectations.
insights.speaker: Taerin Kim
insights.so_what: Convergence of experimental and observational methods raises confidence that the asymmetry is causal, making it a durable input to inflation-expectations models rather than a one-off correlation.
insights.locator: These results are consistent with experimental evidence
